divergence_points.title: Existing rules do not clearly cover the replacement that actually blocked the trial
divergence_points.rationale: The intent says replacement continues under original rules. Closing-review's retry covers a malformed response or transient failure before a conforming verdict exists. The blocked trial excluded a PASS reviewer for an execution-scope violation, then encoded it as conforming=false with malformed-response. The contract defines conforming as structural usability and classifiability, not execution-boundary compliance. Fixing the profile representation alone therefore leaves this replacement dependent on a stretched label. Whether the raw PASS YAML was structurally conforming cannot be verified here.

divergence_points.proposed_change: Add one outcome to the intent: a review excluded for violating its execution boundary supplies no verdict, and its replacement at the same digest is an explicitly defined retry under a stated limit. Leave the failure-kind encoding to the design. If this is rejected, limit Acceptance 2 and 4 to genuinely malformed output and remove the excluded-reviewer case from the claimed repair.

divergence_points.title: Same-reviewer fix verification is merged with failed-attempt replacement
divergence_points.rationale: The intent's Problem and Acceptance 2 treat the initial-event Round 2 run as the same gap as replacement. Fix rounds resume the same agent over a fix delta, while a failed attempt retries without being a round. The resolver returns routed with no next_redispatch on success, and it requires a failure_kind on a conforming failure, so a reviewer correctly reporting code defects has no honest path to a redispatch decision. Counting Rounds 2 and 3 as redispatches also spends the whole budget and leaves no room for a retry in the same reviewer's episode. The report's 'deviation' claim is therefore unsettled: missing Round 1 feedback may be a deviation under the every-completed reading, but an initial event for Round 2 is not proven wrong. The raw log was not supplied.

Add one outcome: the contract states how a same-reviewer review round relates to feedback and the retry budget, and a normal three-round episode must not exhaust that budget. divergence_points.title: Acceptance 4 overpromises completion yet cannot prove the repair
divergence_points.rationale: Acceptance 4 requires completed review and a committed record, while the Proposed outcome allows completion or an explicit stop. Real reviewers may return findings, or a retry may legitimately fail. Passing attestation validation also does not show the feedback path was used: dispatch records stay in active task context, and my search of loom_checker found no dispatch-feedback fields. The study itself reports an attestation that validated without established dispatch conformance.

divergence_points.title: The gap is wider than an unobservable main profile
divergence_points.rationale: Every fallback emits a symbolic effective profile, including with a known main profile: unsupported profiles, host rejection, and a redispatch whose next profile is unsupported. The OpenCode and Antigravity adapters also instruct every dispatch to record host-default/unverified. The reproduction covers only unobservable initial with inheritance guaranteed. A repair keyed to that one path would leave the same stop elsewhere. A fallback's non-null requested_profile also must not be reported as what actually ran.

findings.title: The representation mismatch is a real contract and resolver defect, not caller misuse
findings.rationale: The contract asks for the effective profile, the resolver emits a string in fallback, and the same resolver rejects that string as feedback. The study's trial result also records an attempted null/null pair being rejected, consistent with the model check at line 171. Existing focused tests pass object profiles to after-execution and do not exercise a fallback round trip. Caller interpretation remains in dispute only for the failure label (see the first divergence).

findings.title: Feedback before replacement is mandatory; successful no-retry timing can be settled in the contract
findings.rationale: Feedback before redispatch is explicit. For a success with no retry, 'every completed result' and the requirement that every successful execution returns routed favor mandatory feedback, while 'before any redispatch' still allows the narrower reading. Once success feedback is representable, the dispute no longer blocks work, so Acceptance 1 can stand. The candidate trial's stop also followed an in-flight reminder, so it is not independent proof about ordinary runs.

findings.title: Acceptance does not state what happens to routing failures with unknown settings
findings.rationale: Acceptance 2 is conditional, but it does not say which unknown-state cases stop. Escalation requires a known model and effort, and existing policy already stops when no legal transition exists. Without an explicit outcome, a repair could add a blind retry or an invented escalation. Unknown state can only be retried without overrides where the existing rule is same-profile retry.

findings.title: Two retry ceilings apply, and the intent names neither precisely
findings.rationale: The resolver can return dispatch for malformed output at counts 0 and 1, while closing-review ends the episode after a second failed attempt. The changelog shows this split is deliberate. A rerun that follows only the resolver could exceed the station limit. The resolver is also stateless and trusts the caller's count, so it cannot itself detect a reset.

findings.title: Station retry text and resolver stops already disagree on transient failures
findings.rationale: Closing-review allows one retry after an unavailable executor or other transient failure, but the resolver returns execution-failed for incomplete attempts and non-routing kinds. With relabeling forbidden, such a retry has no legal resolver path. Acceptance 3 says failure stops stay consistent without acknowledging this existing conflict, so a repair could change it silently in either direction.

findings.title: The atomic-pair guarantee has a hole in the path being changed
findings.rationale: Acceptance 3 assumes pair handling already exists on this path. After-execution validates only the model tier, so a known model with a null or non-string effort appears able to reach the success branch and be returned in overrides and effective_profile. This comes from reading the code and was not executed. Adding unknown support here could widen the hole, for example through known-model/unknown-effort input.

findings.title: Truthful unknown state may still be forced into a nonblank model at the attestation boundary
findings.rationale: The finalization input shows a model per verdict, and a delivery-state check rejects a verdict whose model is blank. The contract does not say what an incumbent reviewer with an unknown model should record there. A rerun could therefore pass the resolver and still fabricate at this later boundary. Committed trial attestations were not supplied, so what they recorded is unverified.
